newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON STILL RUNNING FOR PLACE IN HISTORY.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON STILL RUNNING FOR PLACE IN HISTORY.

text.p: Track superstar Michael Johnson has no intention of resting on his Olympic laurels.

"When I finish my career I would like be known as one of all all-time greats of track and field," the 29-year-old double Olympic champion said Friday during a promotional tour for his new book, "Slaying The Dragon".
"For me to be happy and feel that I am one best of all time, I have to be consistent throughout my career," he said.

Johnson's place in Olympic history is surely secure after his unprecedented gold medal performances in the 200 and 400 meters at the Atlanta Games. But he feels that to earn a place among the track immortals, he must keep on winning.

"My desire is not to finish my career as somebody who went to the Olympics and won, but who then lost all the other races, that does not make a great career," said Johnson, who has not had much experience with losing in his stellar career.
"To be great you got to be good time after time," added Johnson, who is unbeaten in his last 57 400 meters finals.

Johnson more than lived up to intensive pre-Olympic hype by not only becoming the first man to win the 200 and 400 at the same Games, but in the way that he accomplished that feat -- with a sizzling 43.39 in the 400 meters and a stunning world record 19.32 seconds in the 200.
Johnson insists, however, that Atlanta was just a stop along the road, albeit in the fast lane.
"If there was no Olympics I would still be a track athlete," he said. "It's not like you train four years for the Olympics and it's all over and done.
"That is kinda of like asking Michael Jordan after winning the (NBA) championship, 'why play?' This is what I do, this is my job, this is how make my living," he said.
The speedster with the unorthodox standup running style plans no more races this year and said he will pass up the 1997 indoor season.
He said he will take to the track again outdoors in April and hopes to soon finalise plans for a big-money match race with Olympic 100 meters champion Donovan Bailey.

Bailey and fellow Canadians were stung when the mythical moniker of world's fastest human, traditionally reserved for the Olympic 100 meters winner, was being used on Johnson during the Summer Games coverage.
A showdown over 150 meters has been tentatively scheduled for May 31 in Toronto, said Johnson, who expects to return to New York City in 1998 to run at the Goodwill Games.
He does not think he will defend both of his titles at the World Championsips in Athens next year. "...not sure 200s or 400s, I don't know which I'll concentrate on."
What he seemed more sure of was the outcome, whichever distance he selects.
"This is how I want to finish my career winning races, not losing races."
